introduction.heading: What is Authentication & Authorization?
introduction.description: Authentication answers "who are you?" - proving a user is who they claim to be, usually with a password, a token, or a login from a third party like Google. Authorization answers a different question - "what are you allowed to do?" - and only makes sense once someone is authenticated. A logged-in user (authenticated) might still get a 403 trying to delete someone else's post (not authorized). Mixing the two up is one of the most common security bugs: checking that a request has a valid token is not the same as checking that the token's owner is allowed to do what they're asking to do.

concepts.title: Password Hashing
concepts.description: Never store passwords in plain text - hash them with bcrypt/argon2 so a database leak doesn't leak passwords

concepts.title: Sessions
concepts.description: Server stores login state and hands the browser an opaque session ID cookie to prove it on future requests

concepts.title: JWTs
concepts.description: A signed, self-contained token the server can verify without a database lookup - common for stateless/API auth

concepts.title: Authorization
concepts.description: Once identity is known, checking what that specific user is allowed to do (roles, ownership, permissions)

concepts.title: OAuth
concepts.description: Let a user prove their identity via a trusted third party (Google, GitHub) instead of your own password system

flow.heading: The Auth Flow
flow.description: Almost every auth system follows the same shape: a user proves their identity once (login), the server hands back some form of proof, and every request after that carries the proof back so the server doesn't have to ask for a password again. What differs between sessions and JWTs is where that proof lives and how it's verified - a session ID is a lookup key into server-side state, while a JWT carries its own verifiable claims and needs no server-side storage at all.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Never store raw passwords - hash them with bcrypt: npm install bcrypt
Pick a strategy: sessions (npm install express-session) or JWTs (npm install jsonwebtoken)
On login, verify the password hash and issue a session cookie or a signed token
Write an auth middleware that checks the cookie/token on protected routes before req reaches the handler
Add an authorization check inside the handler - a valid token proves identity, not permission
For third-party login, use a library like Passport.js or the provider's OAuth SDK rather than hand-rolling OAuth

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: Register, log in, and protect a route with JWTs
fullExample.description: This example wires together password hashing, token issuing, and an auth middleware into one small Express file. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.
code: // 1. Register: hash the password before storing anything
const user = await db.users.create({ email, passwordHash });
// 2. Login: verify the password, then issue a signed token
const token = jwt.sign({ sub: user.id, role: user.role }, SECRET, {
// 3. Middleware: verify the token on every protected request
req.user = jwt.verify(token, SECRET); // throws if invalid or expired
return res.status(403).json({ error: "Not allowed to delete this post" });

steps.label: Hash on register, never store raw passwords
steps.explanation: bcrypt.hash() runs a slow, salted one-way function - even if the database leaks, an attacker gets hashes, not passwords. The plain-text password is never written anywhere.

steps.label: Verify on login with bcrypt.compare()
steps.explanation: You can't reverse a hash back into a password, so login re-hashes the submitted password internally and compares hashes - bcrypt.compare() does this in one call.

steps.label: Issue a signed token
steps.explanation: jwt.sign() bundles the payload (user id, role) with an expiry and signs the whole thing with SECRET. Anyone can read a JWT's payload, but only the server can produce a valid signature for it.

steps.label: Read the token off every request
steps.explanation: By convention the token travels in the Authorization header as "Bearer <token>" - middleware strips that prefix before verifying.

steps.label: Verify, don't just decode
steps.explanation: jwt.verify() checks the signature against SECRET and throws if it's been tampered with or has expired - this is what actually makes a JWT trustworthy, not just its shape.

steps.label: Authentication only proves identity
steps.explanation: requireAuth runs first and guarantees req.user exists and is genuine - but says nothing yet about whether this specific user should be allowed to do this specific thing.

steps.label: Authorization checks the specific action
steps.explanation: Ownership and role are checked inside the handler, against this specific resource - a valid token from any logged-in user isn't enough to delete someone else's post.
